Solar panels use the photovoltaic effect, which Edmond Becquerel discovered in 1839 [1]. Each panel is made of many solar cells, and about 95% of those cells are made of silicon [1]. The silicon is built as two layers, one doped with phosphorus and the other with boron, so the layers have opposite electrical charges [1]. Where the layers meet, a built-in electric field forms [2]. When sunlight hits the cell, light particles (photons) knock electrons loose from their atoms. The electric field pushes those electrons one way, and metal contacts collect them as an electric current [1][2]. More light frees more electrons, so panels produce more power in brighter sun [2].

The current comes out as direct current (DC), so an inverter changes it to the alternating current (AC) that homes and the power grid use [1]. Typical silicon panels turn about 20–23% of the sunlight that hits them into electricity [1]. Compared with photosynthesis, both capture energy from light, but a solar panel turns it straight into electricity rather than storing it in chemical form.
